title: My Half-Marathon ’Fit Check Included Glitter Shadow, Obviously
text:
My Half-Marathon ’Fit Check Included Glitter Shadow, Obviously

As a beauty editor, I’m used to investing a lot of time in my getting-ready routine. But as a relative newcomer to the run community, I quickly learned that running a half marathon requires a whole different kind of getting-ready prep. For Lululemon’s SeaWheeze Half Marathon in the brand’s hometown of Vancouver, Canada, I had to think about everything from sweat-wicking fabrics and chafe-proof shorts to where I’d stash my gels, lip balm, and other race-day essentials. (And, naturally, I also wanted to look cute while doing it!)

Ahead, here’s the full ‘fit check of everything I wore before, during, and after 13.1 miles, from my pre-race 5K warm-up to the post-run massage. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Pre-Race Warm-Up

The day before the half marathon, I joined the Lululemon team and fellow editors for a short-and-sweet 5K. I brought along my tried-and-true Energy Bra (Lululemon, please never discontinue this style!), which I love for its medium support and pretty, streamlined silhouette thanks to the thin straps. On top, I wore one of my many Swiftly Tech Short-Sleeve Shirts, a go-to for any sweaty activity thanks to its odor-resistant silver fibers and soft, airy fabric that moves with you.

I also opted for my new favorite running shorts, the Fast and Free Mid-Rise Split Short 3″. This reimagined take on a Lululemon classic features a new 360° waistband storage system (a huge deal when you’re running!) and an updated performance brief liner that is exceptionally comfortable. The shorts themselves are breezy and lightweight, while the petal-shaped side panels are actually very cute and flattering—a welcome bonus when you’re spending several miles in running gear. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Race Day 

Even though we were in beautiful Vancouver, PNW summer is still summer—which meant I was keeping my race-day kit light and breezy. The hero piece of my outfit was, without a doubt, the Fast and Free Short-Sleeve Shirt, which I wore in a brilliant Yves Klein blue. The fabric is the airiest, most breathable material I’ve ever felt, and it barely showed sweat even when I crossed the finish line. It’s also made with specialized, body-mapped zones of open-knit mesh (aka built-in AC) to ventilate your sweatiest areas—specifically, the back and sleeves. My bra of choice was the Nulux Strappy-Back Sports Bra, B/C Cup (which is currently part of Lululemon’s We Made Too Much section!), which offered medium support with plenty of breathability thanks to its strappy-back design.

My shorts of choice were the Shake It Out High-Rise Running Short, also in the same brilliant blue. I love high-rise, flowy shorts, and this one allowed for unrestricted movement in a flattering, tiered drape that looked so cute on. Maybe my millennial side is showing, but I personally love a high rise: I feel secure and held in, and I don’t have to worry about my waistband riding down while I’m going for a personal best. The shorts also have zippered side pockets, which let me keep a few extra gels on hand without adding bulk—aka potentially slowing me down.

In lieu of a running vest, I opted for the Fast and Free Running Belt, which comes in several fun colorways. (Mine is black, since it goes with everything.) Even though this is probably the slimmest running belt I’ve tried, it was stretchy enough to fit my iPhone 17 easily, along with my mini emotional-support lip balm and glitter shadow (you know, typical running essentials!). The waistband is adjustable, so you can get a snug fit across your hips without it feeling too tight, and it stayed secure without bouncing with every stride. I honestly loved it and am already debating getting another colorway for my next race. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Post-Run Recovery 

Immediately following the race, I showered and changed into my cozy uniform—which was waiting for me on my hotel bed. (Thank you, Lululemon; you think of everything.) Up top was the French Terry Oversized Crew in an elevated neutral beige, which feels like a 2.0 version of the OG Perfectly Oversized Crewneck. I wore my heather gray Little Ribbed Tee underneath, which I’ve been wearing nonstop. It’s Lululemon’s take on a baby tee, but in a soft, ribbed fabric that looks just as good with denim as it does with a silk midi skirt. 

And because I love a matching set, I paired my cozy ‘fit with the French Terry Mid-Rise Short 3.5″, which are made from the same sturdy, matte French terry fabric. Think of them as a fancy, decidedly-not-grubby pair of sweats that wouldn’t look out of place at a luxe hotel spa—which is, conveniently, where I wore them for a post-race massage.

title: How To Dress Like Katseye, According To Your Fave Member Or Upcoming Concert
text:
How To Dress Like Katseye, According To Your Fave Member Or Upcoming Concert

From leather sets and polka dots to knee-high boots and plushies, there are many motifs now synonymous with Katseye’s unique aesthetic. The K-Pop girl group has already gone through several “eras,” or musical chapters, in their two-year career so far. But there’s no doubt that the “Pinky Up” single and accompanying music video cemented their place in the industry as global pop stars, and helped make each member recognizable by her first name alone, à la Addison. To dig deeper into this era’s aesthetic, I spoke with Katseye’s stylist Katie Qian to discuss the members’ cohesive yet chaotic looks and offer tips for fans (AKA Eyekons) who want to dress like Katseye for concerts, festivals, and more.

“The fans are obviously super dedicated on another level, so it makes me really happy when they like the looks and when they’re happy,” Qian tells Refinery29, adding: “From a styling perspective, we usually just focus on doing something that the girls and creative team loves, so when that lands, it’s great that the looks resonate with the people who love Katseye.”

Sharing how the aesthetic differs from the darker, edgier “Gnarly” era, Qian explains: “It’s really just about being fun and whimsical. There’s a lot of motifs in all the looks, like polka dots, always. There’s a bunch of fun textures like tulle and feathers. There’s this bustle element that we’re always bringing in. And then this rave element too of fun, chaotic, maximal layering.” She adds: “The girls love corsets, the girls love bras, and they love to feel sexy and cute.”

For Eyekons to channel the “Pinky Up” aesthetic, Qian suggests: “Any sort of way that the fans can play with what they have in their closet, honestly. Throw unconventional combinations together; mix different textures; and play with a lot of layering, fun cutouts, and asymmetry.” For more inspo, she adds: “The color scheme is usually blues, pinks, pastels, and also bright colors. And always add a wacky fun accessory — something that’s kind of kitschy and out of the box.”

In addition to Qian’s insights, I also took notes from a superfan (AKA my younger sister Sofia) for a breakdown of each member’s signatures that distinguish them from one another, from their style preferences to their cultural influences. Ahead, take inspo from some of Katseye’s most iconic looks since being styled by Qian in late 2025 for The Beautiful Chaos Tour through today with the launch of their Wild EP and new era. Then, shop key styles to put together concert outfits for their performance at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival on August 29 or their WildWorld Tour starting on September 1.  

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Daniela

Lead-dancer Daniela Avanzini (22) comes from Atlanta, Georgia and embraces her Cuban and Venezuelan roots through her fashion and beauty choices. “I need to wear a cross, period. I feel like having a cross around my neck all the time… I feel protected. And it’s part of my childhood and my culture,” Daniela previously told Vogue in a Grammys getting-ready video, also citing seeing her mother wear hoops and reaching for them herself now. My sister also shares that she usually wears chunky sneakers paired with tiny tops and low-rise bottoms for a Y2K feel.

To channel Daniela, opt for edgy leather separates with lots of lace-up details, primary colors (if you’re not going for an all-black look), and chunky jewelry. She also predominantly opts for sets as opposed to bodysuits or dresses, so be sure to elevate your going-out bra top and hot pants game. For the final beauty touch, tightline your eyes with an intense inner eye and wear your hair curly or naturally.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Yoonchae

Yoonchae Jeung (18) serves as Katseye’s “maknae” or youngest member and comes from Seoul, South Korea, making her the only Korean in the K-Pop group. As the baby, she’s often dressed very cutesy, though has hints of a cool “tomboy” style. She told Vogue: “In the ‘Touch’ music video, I was wearing a triangle top and it became my thing,” with her styling team saying that fans always notice triangles on the torso of her outfits, which help give the illusion of an hourglass figure.

To get Yoonchae’s look, consider wearing scarf tops or voluminous mini skirts for an exaggerated hourglass silhouette. She’s often dressed in softer silhouettes, materials, and colors too, so opt for tulle, lace, and pinks when possible. To distinguish herself from her group members, Yoonchae also dyed her hair blonde for an extra light and soft beauty effect. So this may be your call to try the strawberry blonde hair color trend ASAP.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Lara

Main vocalist Lara Raj (20) was born in Connecticut but grew up in Texas and is of Indian and Sri Lankan descent. She brings her cultural identity into her style most prominently through jewelry via her bindis and tikkas, nose ring, and belly ring. “I make sure to go all out with my traditional stuff because it’s so important in that space where there’s so much press and so many photos and so many eyes on us to really represent my culture,” Lara told Vogue. The singer also notably wears many jewel tones and shimmering fabrics to complement her adornments.

Lara sticks to a few core necklines, like halters and sweetheart bra-cups across tops, bodysuits, and gowns, which highlight her chest tattoo. For accessories, if you’re not South Asian, a bindi or tikka may not be doable, but you can still implement crystal hair clips or face gems into your look instead. My sister also pointed out that the singer almost exclusively wears heels, so find a comfortable pair that you can dance the night away in.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Megan

All-rounder Megan Skiendiel (20) who has great range across singing and dancing also has the greatest range in style (and changing hairstyles). Originally from Honolulu, Hawaii, and of Chinese, Singaporean, and Swedish heritage, Megan has an equally varied approach to style. But she told Vogue: “For me, I usually wear my jade bracelet. I never take it off. I’ve had one since I was a kid so it’s a very big thing in Chinese culture.”

While Megan’s aesthetic evolves, she pretty consistently has the most alternative or edgy look, opting for dark eye makeup and hair highlights (including the viral “halo” hair trend). To channel Megan, keep to a color palette of black, white, purples, and reds. And in addition to a jade bracelet, you can also look out for a statement choker necklace, especially when paired with a bandeau-style neckline. Do something wild to your hair, and you’re set.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Sophia

As Katseye’s fan-dubbed leader, Sophia Laforteza (23) was raised in Manila, Philippines. While she’s currently on a wellness hiatus, she’s expected to return in September with more “Wild” era looks. As one of the oldest members of the group, my sister lovingly calls her “Mother,” and explains that Sophia’s style is a bit more sophisticated, polished, and modest at times. Pulling from coquette style, she typically wears lots of ruffles, rosettes, corsets, bloomers, and tulle.

Sophia also often wears halter crop tops across performance costumes and red carpet looks, so consider a halter for casual or fancy ‘fits. Amp up the volume with ruffle-sleeved tops or high-low skirts in pastels or vibrant pinks. Like Lara, Sophia typically prefers sleek heels instead of sneakers or boots, so step into pointy stilettos. And to finish off your look, layer on a juicy pink lip gloss before singing your heart out.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Manon

Manon Bannerman (24), often described by fans as the group’s “visual,” has been on hiatus since February, but her signature aesthetic remains influential among Eyekons. Coming from Switzerland with a multicultural background, she pulls from her Ghanaian roots when it comes to fashion. “I always carry my waist beads with me. I got them in Ghana. It’s just a traditional thing we do in West Africa,” Manon told Vogue, adding: “They’re always on. Sometimes they’re hidden, but they’re like my lucky charm.”

Since we haven’t seen Manon’s take on the “Pinky Up” era, her style within the group is defined by the “Gnarly” era, where she leaned into darker palettes, metallics, lace-up corsets, chunky sneakers, and combat boots. Her ’90s minimalist look is paired back from too many accessories or jewelry — though you can try a waist chain — and is instead highlighted by her dramatic curly hair as the focal point.

title: Lululemon’s Big-Ass Bags Are Actually Kinda Brilliant
text:
Lululemon’s Big-Ass Bags Are Actually Kinda Brilliant

If your feed looks anything like mine, you might have noticed that there’s a new Lululemon drop causing a lot of commotion. No, it’s not another pair of leggings or an unexpected maxi skirt. This time it’s a Big-Ass carryall. That’s not me exaggerating the gargantuan measurements. That’s the actual name of the ludicrously capacious bag.

The banter online is hilarious, with some calling it the everything-AND-the-kitchen-sink bag. But seriously, as a person who hates going back and forth to the car after a grocery store run, this is the brilliant solution for lugging everything at once.

One review agrees, “This bag fits everything my family of 5 needs when traveling. My husband no longer complains about making multiple trips, carrying several bags.” While another one says, “Just throw this bad boy in the shopping cart, leave it open, and shop away! Makes Costco runs a breeze. Kinda wish it was bigger… although now I’m not sure how to get this 400 lbs bag into my car while I stand here in the parking lot… oh well! Lulu will you offer bigger sizes in the future? Thx.” Outside of the functional use cases, fashion has been pushing oversized bags to the forefront of the accessory department for a couple of seasons now.

Just look at Chanel’s Resort 2027 collection and you’ll find a colorful raffia tote that’s nearly the same size as the model carrying it. The intentionally exaggerated proportions were also seen at Altuzarra, Celine, and Stella McCartney—each one proving that it’s kinda chic to be a woman on the go carrying it all.

Of course, this isn’t Lululemon’s only bag that’s causing a frenzy. The girlies have been loving the wear-everywhere belt bags and adorable wristlets for years.

If you’re not quite ready for the 80L Big-Ass bag, Lululemon has some scaled-back versions that aren’t too big nor too small—like the Extra-Large and the Large Slouchy Shoulder Bag. Both of those styles are also perfect for days when you need to tote the necessities, while still ensuring you don’t overpack. title: Shan Boodram On Why You’re Not Getting the Sex You Want and How to Fix It
text:
Shan Boodram On Why You’re Not Getting the Sex You Want and How to Fix It

Shan Boodram is a certified sex educator, board-certified sexologist, and the leading figure in a new kind of sexual education. Wielding an MS in Psychology and a longstanding curiosity, Shan helps people move towards greater intimacy between their partners and themselves. Born and raised in a predominantly white neighborhood in Canada, Shan’s initially poor experiences with sex led her to educate herself on how to prevent these kinds of experiences from occurring again. She built on this curiosity and self-education with professional training and a growing desire to build a new kind of sex ed. Shan joined Naked Beauty Podcast with her usual candor, granting access to her personal experiences with desire, intimacy, sex, and pleasure. During the conversation, Shan made it clear that her goal isn’t just to get people talking about sex, but to take back their power from dominant narratives about sexual development and education to empower ourselves.

Shan walks us through how her loving relationship with her husband exposed her to unconditional love she didn’t realize she was missing. She offers couples tips on how to have a fruitful sex life while managing the responsibilities of long-term partnership, parenting, and the daily drudgery of life. We covered the more unpleasant side of relationships, like how couples can move away from resentment and towards repair. Shan also provided listeners with specific examples that we can employ immediately to have better sex with ourselves and our partners. Shan even offered a live demonstration of her favorite sex positions and toys that are sure to please.

title: I Grew Up Watching Romance Movies Set In Ireland. Then I Found My Own Love Story There
text:
I Grew Up Watching Romance Movies Set In Ireland. Then I Found My Own Love Story There

After a horse-and-carriage ride through Killarney National Park, an enchanted emerald forest in southwestern Ireland, I walked through the old town on the edge of the countryside, my fingers brushing against stone walls as I tried to imagine a history hundreds of years old, mist from a sympathetic raincloud dampening my skin. It felt like a scene ripped from a historical romance screenplay that I’d watch from my living room in Orlando, Florida, charmed and a little envious of the women onscreen, except it was real life. My life.

I was heading back to my hotel with a group of women who had been strangers just a week before. Now, we were co-travelers, bonded by inside jokes and, moments later, a darkening nimbostratus cloud hovering above that made us regret walking the scenic route instead of hailing a taxi.

Then, from a red light, a man driving a horse-drawn carriage noticed the concern in our faces and called out, “Need a lift?” What in my period-drama fantasies was happening? The four of us looked at one another, giggled, and — as women of the 21st-century, liberated from strict social codes and calling card etiquette — decided to do it for the shelter and the plot. Darting through traffic, we climbed aboard the rig, where three Irish gentlemen greeted us and whisked us back toward our hotel.

Growing up, I fell in love with Ireland because it was the setting of so many of my favorite romance films. “P.S. I Love You” taught me that romance would arrive the moment I, the reserved, goody-two-shoes, threw back a shot of Jameson, let my hair down, and did something feral like sing terribly at a small-town pub. “Leap Year” showed me that love would come when I embraced folktales and whimsicality, sparking a decadeslong desire to roll down the country’s lush, billowing hills. “Brooklyn” helped me realize that great love could appear in unexpected people, places, and times in our lives. 

So when I decided to take EF Ultimate Break’s Women Traveling Solo trip, I knew I’d go to Ireland. Long ago, the portrayals of the verdant country in 2000s- and 2010s-era romance flicks stole my heart — and all these years later, the young hopeless romantic in me still hoped for my very own Irish love story.

During the nine-day excursion, which I did alongside 20-plus young women from all over the U.S., we traveled throughout the country, with overnight stays in Dublin, Kilkenny, Killarney, and Galway. In each city, I lived like the protagonists of those films, open to the mysterious journeys that lay ahead and hungry for adventure. I also felt unencumbered. Liberation felt contagious in that socialist country that fought long and hard for its own sovereignty, allowing me to similarly feel free in both my body and spirit.

I spent my first night in Dublin pub-hopping through Temple Bar, the lively cultural quarter in Central Dublin, eventually shimmying my way into the perpetually packed tourist stop The Temple Bar Pub. Inside, I ducked to dodge overflowing pints of Guinness held above my head and grabbed onto strangers when I slipped on beer spilled on the sticky floor. Eventually, I made it to a small table in front of the stage, where a band was playing a series of songs from the movie “Grease.” Beside me was a tall, blond English man who was also there on holiday and told me he had played Danny in his high school play. That night, I became his Sandy. The two of us sang-yelled our way through the cheesy ’70s classics like we meant every melodramatic lyric. It was a motion picture-style meet-cute, reminiscent of that pub scene in “P.S. I Love You” where Gerry (Gerard Butler) sings “Galway Girl” to Holly (Hilary Swank). We laughed and took videos of our performance. And then I slipped out the side door, joining my group of travelers outside, knowing we’d never see each other again, knowing I didn’t want to. That playful coquetry was enough for me.

When my feet began to throb after miles of walking on cobblestone streets, a few of the girls I had just met that morning offered to walk back to the hotel with me, one even stopping every other block to wait when I needed a break and insisting I stop apologizing every time I told her how sorry and embarrassed I was to be that girl.

* * *

The next day, we embarked on a walking tour, me in REI hiking boots that were much more suitable for the rock-paved roads than the previous night’s heels. Walking along a bridge over the River Liffey, where Viking fleets once sailed, raided, and established a settlement that would become Dublin more than a thousand years ago, we learned about Ireland’s long, brutal history of colonization. 

At Dublin Castle, we were told about the Norman invasion of Ireland and how, after arriving in 1169, the Anglo-Normans began establishing their foothold in Dublin, eventually using the castle as a defensive fortification. Over the centuries, the English Crown expanded its control across Ireland, and the castle became the center of English, and eventually British, rule. There, the Lord Lieutenant, the British monarch’s representative in Ireland, governed on behalf of the Crown, overseeing the administration of everything from government, land, policing, religion, and courts. 

For Irish nationalists, the castle came to embody violent colonial power. In 1916, Irish republicans attempted to seize Dublin Castle as part of their effort to overthrow British rule in a rebellion now remembered as the Easter Rising. While rebels, a mix of revolutionary artists, teachers, and political organizers, failed to capture it — and its leaders, including the poet Patrick Pearse and labor organizer James Connolly, were executed — the failed uprising ultimately ignited the movement that led to Irish independence.

As a Puerto Rican, whose homeland was also colonized by a European imperial power, Spain, before being invaded and seized by the United States — which still maintains control over the archipelago — this history deeply resonated with me. Throughout the trip, I began drawing parallels between our islands’ histories of colonization and resistance. 

Both have experienced brutality from their colonizers, from massacres of our nationalist leaders, to the seizure and contamination of our lands, to attempts to suppress our languages and cultures.

Both were also abandoned amid devastating crises. During the Great Famine, Ireland was forced to continue exporting food to Great Britain even as its people starved, with about 1 million people dying. Nearly two centuries later, when Hurricane María wrecked Puerto Rico in 2017, the island’s colonial status and the failures of the federal response compounded the catastrophe. A Harvard study found there were 4,645 deaths in the months following the storm, many of them attributed to delayed or prevented medical care.

Similarly, both islands were emptied by these histories, creating diasporas that today outnumber the populations living on the islands themselves.

Understanding this shared history, when our tour guide walked us to a building with The Proclamation of the Irish Republic scrawled on its wall, he called on me to read a passage: “We declare the right of the people of Ireland to the ownership of Ireland and to the unfettered control of Irish destinies, to be sovereign and indefeasible. The long usurpation of that right by a foreign people and government has not extinguished the right, nor can it ever be extinguished except by the destruction of the Irish people.” 

He then looked at me and said something like, “May this be an inspiration for you and the Puerto Rican people to never stop fighting for a freedom that belongs to you.” With goosebumps bubbling all over my skin and my eyelids heavy with tears, I thanked him, remembering all I knew about Puerto Rican and Irish solidarity, from nationalist leader Pedro Albizu Campos studying the Irish independence movement to Irish-American lawyers representing Puerto Rican freedom fighters.

* * *

Later that night, at an old pub, I asked the musician serenading us tourists to perform The Cranberries’ “Linger,” slipping him a few euros in hopes he’d move it up on his setlist. It’s one of the many songs by the Irish band that I sing as passionately today as I did in the ’90s, now with the lived experience of knowing what it actually feels like to long for someone who is no good for you.

Making my way back to my seat with the rest of the girls, a group of men stopped me to chat. They asked where I was from, and when I responded, “Orlando,” the table erupted. They lived there, too. We started tossing out the names of high schools we attended and streets we lived on, surprised to have found one another thousands of miles away, in a centuries-old pub in Dublin. 

A man with a Dominican flag stitched onto his hat asked how long I’d be in the city. When I told him I’d be leaving for Kilkenny in the morning, he asked for my number. I gave him my Instagram handle instead. For the next 45 minutes, we smiled flirtatiously at each other, brushing against one another when “Linger” finally came on and I got up to sing and dance along. 

When I headed out to the next pub with my co-travelers, he gave me a goodbye kiss on the cheek, a customary caribeño farewell. But by the time I was back in my hotel room, there was something else: a DM asking me to stay one more night so we could see why fate brought the Puerto Rican and Dominican from Orlando together in Dublin. I felt him. Like Anna (Amy Adams) and Declan (Matthew Goode) from “Leap Year,” it seemed like our paths crossed for a reason. But, in real life, I wasn’t as invested in figuring out why. There were castles, fairy folklore, and the Cliffs of Moher ahead on our itinerary. I politely declined. 

I spent the rest of the trip gallivanting around the country with strangers who became mates whose coffee orders I remembered, photo angles I learned, and real-life worries I held. Together, we skipped across the rocks at the Lower Lake in Glendalough, pausing to stop and stare at gentle sheep, each of us in awe of the landscape we had only ever seen in pastoral Impressionist paintings. We twirled from Kilkenny Castle to Blarney Castle, simultaneously imagining ourselves as ladies of the court while critiquing the colonial wealth. When we made our way by horse-and-carriage to Ross Castle in Killarney, the women, who knew how desperately I wanted to roll down Ireland’s grassy hills, pointed out a safe place for me to make my childhood dream come true, right in front of the medieval ruin, even capturing my youthful awe and giggles as I went round and round on video. We petted a lamb named Snowy, hugged mossy trees, nearly flew away in the winds at the Cliffs of Moher, attempted our best kicks after watching a Celtic stepdance performance, and spun together amid the wildflowers, 330 feet above the Atlantic, on Inis Mór.

At Kyteler’s Inn, a public house in Kilkenny dating back to the 13th or 14th century, three of us sat down for dinner. We went because we were fascinated by the tale of a woman who once lived there, Dame Alice Kyteler, the first person to be condemned for witchcraft in Ireland after she was accused of bewitching and killing her husbands. But it was the local band that evening that kept us in our seats for hours. They sang story-driven folk songs. Some were call-and-response, and we learned to clap or yell back at the lyrics on cue. Others were too fast-paced for us to understand, but we laughed, overjoyed, nonetheless. But it was their performance of “Grace” that brought me to tears. The song is sung from the point of view of Joseph Plunkett, an Irish freedom fighter and leader of the 1916 Easter Rising. In it, he sings to his longtime sweetheart, Grace Gifford, whom he married in his prison cell just hours before he was scheduled to be executed by a British firing squad.

The song broke me. A tragic 20th-century Irish romance? That’s my kind of period drama. A real-life story of saying goodbye to someone you love far too soon? That’s a pain I know. A love for land, culture, and people so deep, a vision of freedom even after hundreds of years of cruel captivity? That’s a struggle I resonate with. 

Ireland is a land of romance, not just because of the Hollywood films that use its verdant fields and folklore as backdrops for some of my favorite cinematic love stories, but because love has guided its people for generations. 

Love is what fueled their fight for liberation amid massacres, oppression, and starvation. Love is what helped shape a socialist government rooted in equality and collective care. It’s why relatives still scarred by the trauma of the Famine ask, “Do you have enough?” instead of “How’s the food?” when feeding their communities. And it’s why so many in Ireland, just like others in Puerto Rico, are looking back and reclaiming languages, histories, cultures, agricultural practices, and folktales, unearthing what colonialism tried to bury.

* * *

We spent our last day of the trip in Galway, a bohemian seaport city on Ireland’s scenic west coast. It’s here that the Claddagh ring — a traditional Irish piece of jewelry featuring a heart to represent love, a crown to symbolize loyalty, and two clasped hands representing friendship — was first designed hundreds of years ago. While there are many legends surrounding the ring’s origins, it has been used for centuries to signal the wearer’s romantic relationship status. Depending on which hand it’s worn on and which direction the heart faces, the ring can reveal whether someone is single, in a relationship, engaged, or married.

Earlier in our Grand Tour of Ireland trip, a few of us decided to wait to buy our Claddagh rings until we made it to Galway, wanting to purchase them where the ring and myth were born. I bought a gold one with a delicate frame. That night, I wore mine at the beer garden at O’Connell’s Bar. It was on my right hand, with the heart facing outward, indicating that I was single and open to romance. And I found it. Not with the Irish gentleman who saved a damsel in distress on horse-and-carriage, not with the English millennial version of Danny Zuko, and not with the dominicano who apparently lives a few blocks away from where I grew up. I found it in the warmth of women-only travel and the enchanting rolling hills of Ireland.

That night, I sang nostalgic American pop hits at the top of my lungs with a group of women whom I might have gone a lifetime without ever knowing, on an island filled with beauty and heart that colonization tried, but failed, to extinguish. This is love, too.

This story was reported on a trip provided by EF Ultimate Break.

title: The One Skirt Taking Office & Weekend Slays To The Next Level
text:
The One Skirt Taking Office & Weekend Slays To The Next Level

As the sad beige phase dwindles down, there’s a clear hue that’s rising to the top of fashion’s ranks, and it has major staying power. We’ve seen pops of red show up time and time again, but designers are constantly finding ways to revive the pigment and make it feel more relevant than ever. Most of the trends taking over the streets can be traced back to the runway.

A few years ago, it was The Row’s firetruck sweater that hypnotized the fashion scene. Then, Maximilian Davis invigorated Ferragamo’s red leather on Hug bags and sculptural heels. Most recently, the brightest star was seen on the Fall/Winter 2026-2027 runways in Tory Burch’s collection: a patent leather red pencil skirt, smartly paired with a neutral cardigan tucked into the drop waist and anchored with black pumps and a white bag.

Red skirts are the superstars of some of the best street-style looks this season. Whether it’s a sharp knee-length design as seen on Tracee Ellis Ross and Ashley Graham, or it’s a shirred and fringed rendition à la Ava Dash and H.E.R., that dopamine-inducing color never seems to fail sartorially.

If you’re looking for ways to brighten up your own wardrobe, especially as we transition from summer to fall, start with a classic pencil skirt. The timeless silhouette will breathe new life into your office wardrobe. Pair it with a crisp button-down shirt or your favorite autumn sweater for instant street-style-star vibes. Keep your kitten heel sandals in rotation or go sporty chic with sleek retro sneakers.

On the other side of the spectrum, you can have fun with voluminous bubble hem red skirts or ruffled designs. Those will take you from brunch to parties and everything in between. Style them with graphic tees, tanks, or coordinating tops.

To make your hunt for the perfect red skirt easier, I’m dropping my faves ahead. From Tory Burch’s viral vibrant runway design to the affordable yet superb quality of Alex Mill, your next red-hot look is just a click away.

title: Katseye’s Stylist Talks The K-Pop Group’s Evolving Aesthetics & “Pinky Up” Era
text:
Katseye’s Stylist Talks The K-Pop Group’s Evolving Aesthetics & “Pinky Up” Era

Reality TV competition series have surprisingly manufactured some significant girl groups over the years, from MTV’s Danity Kane to The X Factor’s Little Mix and Fifth Harmony to K-pop group Twice. And their signature styles were often as influential as their music. The latest, greatest girl group to come out of such a show is Katseye. Spawned from “The Debut: Dream Academy” — a real-time performance competition that selected and trained individuals to form a global girl group — the six members of Katseye officially debuted (fittingly with their single “Debut”) in June 2024. And they’ve been breaking boundaries and defying expectations ever since.

The original members (and their fan-dubbed roles) are leader Sophia Laforteza, main vocalist Lara Raj, lead dancer Daniela Avanzini, visual symbol Manon Bannerman, all-rounder Megan Skiendiel, and “maknae” or youngest member Yoonchae Jeung. Though they come from South Korea, the Philippines, Switzerland, and the United States — and have South Asian, Chinese, and Latin American roots — and predominantly sing in English, the group is considered K-pop because of its specific training system.

From distinctive “eras” and viral dance routines (who doesn’t know their Gap denim commercial or “Pinky Up” music video at this point?) to monumental festival debuts and even more surprising hiatuses, Katseye has rocked the world in the two years that it’s existed. To take a deeper dive into the group’s evolving eras and unique fashion aesthetics, I previously spoke to celebrity stylist Katie Qian — who also styles the likes of Tyla, Alysa Liu, and Conan Gray — ahead of Katseye’s Governors Ball debut. Ahead, she gives insight into the girl group’s already-iconic outfits (with a look inside Qian’s camera) and shares what she has in store for them next (in their “Wild” era).

Photos: Jeremychanphotography/Getty Images, Kevin Winter/Getty Images.

While she didn’t work with Katseye straight out of “Dream Academy,” Qian started styling the group in late 2025 for The Beautiful Chaos Tour. There, she joined forces with creative director Humberto Leon and visual director Joao Moraes to craft a distinctive, cohesive look for the members.

“Being thrown into the Katseye world, there’s just a lot to learn because there’s so many girls and a lot of creatives involved. It’s been really fun developing that aesthetic for them,” Qian tells Refinery29. “Humberto and I connected and we were really excited to work together in the ‘Gnarly’ era,” Qian says. 

This era, or musical chapter, includes singles like “Gnarly” and “Gabriela” along with The Beautiful Chaos Tour. At the time, the girls were styled in bold black ‘fits. “‘Gnarly’ was a lot of dark tones, a lot of leather, and hardware. I would say it’s more of a dark and edgy era,” Qian adds. Think: black leather sets, lots of plaid, animal prints and fur, grommets, pinstripe suits, denim, and fiery reds. 

But there’s a big distinction for Qian when styling for a tour versus a music video versus a red carpet. “For tour, there’s just a lot more to consider when we are creating the looks. These girls are dancing, doing insane choreography, they’re doing stunts. So when we’re creating the tour looks, it’s really functionality first and it needs to be really performance-friendly,” Qian explains. “And the looks also need to withstand the test of time if they’re dancing for two hours every single night for a few months.”

Photos: Katie Qian.

Post-tour, the next big styling moments came at the top of 2026 with Spotify’s annual Best New Artist Party and the 68th Grammy Awards, where the group gave a glimpse of departing from its previous era’s dark palettes. “I definitely am always just on the lookout for designers I think would be a good fit for Katseye. It’s definitely a niche. I’m looking for specific people who are able to create a bunch of different looks that look cohesive together,” Qian explains.

For the Spotify nominees’ red carpet looks, the members stunned in crystal-adorned mermaidcore designs from luxury Lebanese designer Georges Hobeika. Each member wore a distinctive gown or matching set in silver, pale pink, or deep green, creating the effect of a glamorous fairy tribe.

Then for the Grammys red carpet, Qian followed a similar formula, pulling from one designer (Ludovic de Saint Sernin) and focusing on the same colors and fabrics (white lace and leather, plus silver crystal mesh) across the six members for a cohesive girl group look. “For award shows, we just keep it more refined usually because on the carpet, I feel like things translate completely differently than if it’s in a video or in concept photos that we’re taking,” Qian explains, adding: “We just try to make all of them look nice standing next to each other. It has to be a bit more refined and sophisticated looking, and not too overwhelming.” (Though for their actual Grammys “Gnarly” performance, they dressed in accordance to the era with Kim Possible-esque Off-White utilitarian costumes.) 

Photos: Rich Polk/Getty Images, Gilbert Flores/Getty Images.

Then in a surprising turn of events, it was announced on February 20 that Manon would be taking a hiatus to focus on her mental health. But with a full schedule of music video drops and festival season on the docket, the remaining five members were still ready to give us great performances and even greater looks.

Their Lollapalooza Chile and Festival Estéreo Picnic performances in March still tied to the “Gnarly” aesthetic and era, but focused more on metallic blues, bold ketchup and mustard combos, and animal print rather than head-to-toe black. But then, we entered a completely new era.

On April 9, Katseye released their next single and music video, “Pinky Up,” which perhaps catapulted the group most into the cultural zeitgeist. The upbeat song and quick-paced choreography meshed with outlandish costumes, creating a viral moment.

“Music videos are my favorite because we can go really crazy and conceptual with the looks. For ‘Pinky Up,’ I felt like we could make all of our wildest dreams come true, because although they are doing choreography, it’s not live,” Qian says. “There’s also a concept for a music video, so it’s really fun to tell a story with the looks.

“The ‘Pinky Up’ music video had this overarching tea party but made rave and chaotic kind of vibe. It’s just really vibrant, a lot of layering, and really kitschy and maximal,” Qian explains. “But then obviously we take each girl’s preferences into consideration, and they get to pick which looks they wear.”

This truly felt like the first time each member got distinctive looks that really stood apart from each other and were as dynamic as their personalities with lots of color, texture, and quirky accessorizing. Aside from one scene where the group wears the exact same Fembot-inspired outfits and blonde wigs, each girl wore multiple looks just as out-there as the next. Qian shares: “I think the looks from the ‘Pinky Up’ music video are my favorite. I just felt like they have character to them, and it’s like diving into a whole new world because that was the first peek of their new era.”

Photos: Katie Qian.

This era came just one day before the group’s Coachella debut where they got to perform the immediate-hit song, donning Alice in Wonderland-coded pastel striped and polka-dotted bra and short sets during Weekend 1, and Victoria’s Secret Angel-coded nude and pink lingerie looks for Weekend 2. This was just the start for their monumental “Pinky Up” era and aesthetic.

“The first weekend of Coachella was kind of psycho tea party vibes. And for the AMAs, we had this plushy concept. And now for Gov Ball, we’re doing something that really dives into this polka dot concept that we have been exploring in the ‘Pinky Up’ era,” Qian explains. To get the aesthetic down, Qian brought in Vietnamese brand La Lune to create the statement-making looks for all of these performances.

Photos: Katie Qian.

Since Governor’s Ball, Katseye released their single and music video “Animal” in July where we got a peek into a moodier, businesscore aesthetic (similar to “Gnarly”) for the upcoming “Wild” era. In August, the group also announced a short hiatus for Sophia’s health before the four reamaining members performed at a couple of music festivals, wearing looks that felt like a hybrid of “Pinky Up” pastels and prints with contrasting “Wild” blacks.

“My favorite part of the styling process is probably just getting to realize all these crazy visions that we have in our heads. Humberto and I will just be chatting on the phone like: ‘What should we do that’s never been seen before?’ Qian shares. At the time of speaking with the stylist, she couldn’t divulge much about the next era. “For Wild, I don’t know yet, actually. I can’t say just yet, but I’m sure that Humberto and Joao are thinking of some really fun ideas for us to explore in the ‘Wild’ Era.”

And with Katseye’s documentary Wild Hearts releasing today, their EP Wild launching on August 14, plus a world tour kicking off on September 1, we’re in for an era upgrade and a lot more wild style.

Photo: Katie Qian. | Header photos: Rich Polk/Getty Images, Kevin Mazur/Getty Images.

Look out for Refinery29’s upcoming shopping guide to get Katseye’s look, according to Qian, whether you’re attending their WildWorld Tour or channeling a bold and wild fall.
